title: Exercise Alone Can Address Six of the 14 Modifiable Risk Factors for Dementia, a New Study Finds
excerpt: Researchers at the University of Minnesota say consistent physical activity can prevent or delay up to half of all dementia cases — and a telehealth pilot proved it works even in rural communities with no gym access.
body:
Roughly 42 per cent of Americans over 55 will eventually develop some form of dementia. The number of new diagnoses per year is projected to double between 2020 and 2060. But a growing body of research — highlighted this month during Alzheimer's and Brain Health Awareness Month — suggests that a staggering proportion of those cases don't have to happen at all.

A study from the University of Minnesota School of Nursing has identified 14 modifiable risk factors for cognitive decline. What makes the finding remarkable is how many of those risk factors converge on a single intervention: six of the 14 can be directly addressed through consistent physical exercise.

## One Intervention, Six Risk Factors

Dereck Salisbury, an associate professor at the university and lead researcher, laid out the mechanism in practical terms. Regular exercise simultaneously mitigates obesity, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, depression, high cholesterol, and physical inactivity. These six conditions are interconnected — each one amplifies the others — and together they account for a large share of preventable dementia risk.

"By managing these interconnected health conditions, individuals can protect their vascular health, reduce systemic inflammation, and lower the likelihood of premature cognitive decline," Salisbury said.

The remaining eight modifiable risk factors include social isolation, hearing loss, excessive alcohol use, traumatic brain injury, air pollution, lower education levels, smoking, and poor diet. While exercise doesn't directly fix all of these, its effects on mood, social engagement (especially in group settings), and metabolic health create a foundation that makes addressing the others easier.

## The Telehealth Pilot That Proved It Works in Rural America

To test whether exercise-based prevention could work outside well-resourced urban environments, Salisbury's team ran a telehealth pilot targeting adults aged 45 and older in rural communities — people who were already worried about their memory but had no easy access to gyms, neurologists, or specialised wellness programmes.

Participants were enrolled in a virtual exercise programme and provided with home equipment: stationary cycles, heart rate monitors, and blood pressure cuffs. Researchers monitored their progress through virtual health screenings.

After three months of structured training, participants showed significant improvements in aerobic fitness. The researchers noted that the format — accessible, remote, equipment-supported — could be replicated at scale, including in underserved communities across the developing world.

## The Evidence Is Now Converging From Multiple Directions

The Minnesota findings align with a wider body of research published over the past two years. A study from the Framingham Heart Study, published in *JAMA Network Open*, found that moderate-to-heavy physical activity in midlife was associated with a 35 to 38 per cent lower risk of dementia. Heavy exercise was linked to a 34 per cent reduction. The benefits were most pronounced for those without the APOE ε4 gene variant — the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's.

A separate analysis from the Health and Retirement Study, which emulated a clinical trial using observational data from over 1,500 participants, found that physical activity initiated from midlife reduced dementia risk by up to 49 per cent under the most adherent conditions.

And NIH-funded research in animal models has shown that exercise restores gene activity in brain cells affected by Alzheimer's — particularly in oligodendrocyte progenitor cells that produce the myelin sheath protecting neurons — and activates disease-associated microglia that help clean up the damage.

## Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora

Dementia rates among South Asians remain underreported, but the risk profile is alarming. The community's elevated rates of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease — all independent dementia risk factors — mean that the 14-factor framework applies with particular force.

Cultural barriers compound the problem. Exercise is still undervalued as a health intervention in many South Asian households, particularly among older adults who may view structured physical activity as something for the young. The stigma around cognitive decline can also delay diagnosis by years, reducing the window for prevention.

The Minnesota telehealth model offers a template that could be adapted for NRI communities and even exported to India, where access to neurological care is heavily skewed toward urban centres. A home-based, remotely monitored exercise programme requires no specialist infrastructure — just a will to start.

## The Bottom Line

The researchers' core message is deliberately simple: it is never too late to begin exercising, but the earlier you start, the more you stand to gain. Aerobic exercise, strength training, and mind-body activities all enhance cognition, executive function, and short-term memory. The specific modality matters less than consistency.

"For the intervention to be truly sustainable, it needs to be an activity that the individual genuinely enjoys," Salisbury said. "Finding a personalised, engaging routine is the most effective way to ensure long-term compliance and protect brain health for the future."

For a community that already faces elevated metabolic and cardiovascular risk, treating exercise not as optional wellness but as a non-negotiable form of neuroprotection may be the single most impactful health decision available.
